question.problem: Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, find the maximum value of the sum of the cosines of three non-negative angles whose sum is $\frac{\pi }{2}.$
question.worked_solution:
Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the measures of the angles. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡z,
$$

subject to the constraint

$$
x+y+z=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

We also have the constraints $0\le x,y,z\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=x+y+z.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=\frac{\pi }{2}
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,-\operatorname{sin}⁡y,-\operatorname{sin}⁡z⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x=\lambda  \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡y=\lambda  \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡z=\lambda \end{aligned}
$$

From the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the sine function is one-to-one on the interval $[0,\frac{\pi }{2}],$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y=x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =\frac{\pi }{2} \\ x+x+x & =\frac{\pi }{2} \\ 3x & =\frac{\pi }{2} \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{2},0,0) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =2 \\  & <f(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}).\end{aligned}
$$
